$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 - 4}}\, \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left(\frac {x}{2} \right)^2 - 1}} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}u = \arcosh{u}+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $\left(\dfrac {x}{2} \right)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u = \dfrac {x}{2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $4$ | $2\sqrt{5}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $2$ | $\sqrt{5}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\eqalign{
\int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 - 4}}\, \textrm{d}x &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left(\frac {x}{2} \right)^2 - 1}} \, \textrm{d}x \[5pt]

&= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{2}^{\sqrt 5} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{u^2 - 1}} \cdot (2 \, \textrm{d}u) \[5pt]

&= \int_{2}^{\sqrt 5} \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\sqrt{u^2 - 1}} \[5pt]

&= \arcosh u \Big|_{2}^{\sqrt 5} \[5pt]

&= \arcosh{\sqrt 5} - \arcosh{2} \[5pt]

&=  \ln\left(\sqrt 5 + \sqrt{\left(\sqrt 5\right)^2 - 1}\right) - \ln\left(2 + \sqrt{\left(2\right)^2 - 1}\right)  \[5pt]

&= \ln\left(2 + \sqrt{5}\right) -  \ln\left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right)  \[5pt]

& = \ln\left(\dfrac{2 + \sqrt{5}}{2 + \sqrt{3}}  \right)

}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

EXPLANATION

Let's rewrite our integral as

∫1x2+3dx=13∫1(x3)2+1dx

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine, ∫1u2+1du=arsinh⁡u+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have (x3)2.

So, let's substitute u=x3. Differentiating, we get dudx=13⟹dx=3du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and compute it, as follows: ∫1x2+3dx=13∫1(x3)2+1dx=13∫1u2+1⋅3du=∫duu2+1=arsinh⁡u+C=arsinh⁡(x3)+C

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Sine
content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Substitute u=e^{2x}, so du=2e^{2x} dx and e^{4x}=u². The integral becomes ∫du/√(u²+1)=arsinh(u)+C, giving arsinh(e^{2x})+C.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${e}^{4x}={({e}^{2x})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u={e}^{2x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2{e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2{e}^{2x}}{\sqrt{{e}^{4x}+1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{2{e}^{2x}}{\sqrt{{({e}^{2x})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{2u}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡{e}^{2x}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $7{x}^{2}={(\sqrt{7}\,x)}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{7}\,x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{7}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{7{x}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{{(\sqrt{7}\,x)}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(\sqrt{7}\,x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

∫1u2+1du=arsinh⁡u+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have 7x2=(7x)2.

So, let's substitute u=7x. Differentiating, we get dudx=7⟹dx=17du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and compute it, as follows: ∫77x2+1dx=∫7(7x)2+1dx=∫7u2+1⋅(17du)=∫1u2+1du=arsinh⁡u+C=arsinh⁡(7x)+C

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Sine
content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $7{x}^{2}={(\sqrt{7}\,x)}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{7}\,x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{7}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{7{x}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{{(\sqrt{7}\,x)}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(\sqrt{7}\,x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Sine
content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

 

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $36{x}^{2}=(6x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=6x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{36{x}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{(6x)^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsinh}⁡6x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-25}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{5}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=5\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-25}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot 5\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(\frac{x}{5})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=3x, so du=3 dx. The integral becomes ∫du/√(u²−1)=arcosh(3x)+C on x>1/3, giving option a. On x<−1/3, a real antiderivative is −arcosh(−3x)+C.

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $9{x}^{2}=(3x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{9{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{(3x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcosh}⁡3x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

∫1u2−1du=arcosh⁡u+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have 9x2=(3x)2.

So, let's substitute u=3x. Differentiating, we get dudx=3⟹dx=13du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and compute it, as follows:

∫39x2−1dx=3∫1(3x)2−1dx=3∫1u2−1⋅13du=∫1u2−1du=arcosh⁡u+C=arcosh⁡3x+C

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{7}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-49}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{7}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{7}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=7\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-49}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot 7\,\text{d}u \\  & =7\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =7\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =7\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(\frac{x}{7})+C\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine, ∫1u2−1du=arcosh⁡u+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have (x7)2.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine
content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{7}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-49}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{7}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{7}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=7\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-49}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot 7\,\text{d}u \\  & =7\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =7\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =7\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(\frac{x}{7})+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-8}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{8}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{8}})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{2}})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{2}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{2\sqrt{2}}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-8}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{2}})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{2}})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-8}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{2}})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{2}})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

EXPLANATION

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

∫1u2−1du=arcosh⁡u+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have 16x2=(4x)2.

So, let's substitute u=4x. Differentiating, we get dudx=4⟹dx=14du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and compute it, as follows:

∫116x2−1dx=∫1(4x)2−1dx=∫1u2−1⋅14du=14∫1u2−1du=14arcosh⁡u+C=14arcosh⁡4x+C

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine
content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $16{x}^{2}=(4x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{(4x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡4x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=x/√7, so dx=√7 du. Then the integral is 3√7∫du/(1−u²)=3√7 artanh(x/√7)+C, valid for |x|<√7. This is option b.

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{21}{7-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=3\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{7}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{21}{7-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{7}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\sqrt{7}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1-{u}^{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{7}\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C \\  & =3\sqrt{7}\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})+C\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}}|<1.$

Let's rewrite our integral as ∫217−x2dx=3∫11−(x7)2dx.

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent, ∫11−u2du=artanh⁡u+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have (x7)2.

So, let's substitute u=x7. Differentiating, we get dudx=17⟹dx=7du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and compute it, as follows: ∫217−x2dx=3∫11−(x7)2dx=3∫11−u2⋅7du=37∫du1−u2=37artanh⁡u+C=37artanh⁡(x7)+C

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x7|<1.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent
content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{21}{7-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=3\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{7}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{21}{7-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{7}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\sqrt{7}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1-{u}^{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{7}\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C \\  & =3\sqrt{7}\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})+C\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}}|<1.$

after.name: Question 12
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{12}{16-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{3}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{4}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{12}{16-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 4\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1-{u}^{2}} \\  & =3\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C \\  & =3\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{x}{4})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let's rewrite our integral as ∫1216−x2dx=34∫11−(x4)2dx.

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent, ∫11−u2du=artanh⁡u+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have (x4)2.

So, let's substitute u=x4. Differentiating, we get dudx=14⟹dx=4du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and compute it, as follows: ∫1216−x2dx=34∫11−(x4)2dx=34∫11−u2⋅4du=3∫du1−u2=3artanh⁡u+C=3artanh⁡(x4)+C

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x4|<1.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option c for |x|<4. Differentiating 3 artanh(x/4) gives (3/4)/(1−x²/16)=12/(16−x²), exactly the integrand. The deliberately incorrect submission selected option d.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent
content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{12}{16-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{3}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{4}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{12}{16-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 4\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1-{u}^{2}} \\  & =3\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C \\  & =3\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{x}{4})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x}{4}|<1.$

decision.explanation: Let u=x/3, so dx=3 du. The integral becomes (5/3)∫du/(1−u²)=(5/3)artanh(x/3)+C, valid for |x|<3. Thus option d is correct.

after.name: Question 13
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{5}{9-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{5}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{9-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{5}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1-{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x}{3}|<1.$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent, ∫11−u2du=artanh⁡u+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have (x3)2.

So, let's substitute u=x3. Differentiating, we get dudx=13⟹dx=3du.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent
content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{5}{9-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{5}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{9-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{5}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1-{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x}{3}|<1.$

after.name: Question 14
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{2}{4-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{4-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1-{u}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x}{2}|<1.$

∫24−x2dx=

a
14artanh⁡(x2)+C
b
artanh⁡(x2)+C
c
4artanh⁡(x4)+C
d
2artanh⁡(x4)+C
e
12artanh⁡(x4)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's rewrite our integral as ∫24−x2dx=12∫11−(x2)2dx.

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent, ∫11−u2du=artanh⁡u+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have (x2)2.

So, let's substitute u=x2. Differentiating, we get dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and compute it, as follows: ∫24−x2dx=12∫11−(x2)2dx=12∫11−u2⋅2du=∫du1−u2=artanh⁡u+C=artanh⁡(x2)+C

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x2|<1.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option b for |x|<2. Differentiating artanh(x/2) gives (1/2)/(1−x²/4)=2/(4−x²), exactly the integrand. The deliberately incorrect submission selected option c.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent
content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{2}{4-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{4-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1-{u}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x}{2}|<1.$

after.name: Question 15
after.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $16{x}^{2}=(4x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{12}{1-16{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =12\int \frac{1}{1-(4x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =12\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C \\  & =3\operatorname{artanh}⁡4x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|4x|<1.$

d

Correct
EXPLANATION

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent, ∫11−u2du=artanh⁡u+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have 16x2=(4x)2.

So, let's substitute u=4x. Differentiating, we get

dudx=4⟹14du=dx.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate it, as follows:

∫121−16x2dx=12∫11−(4x)2dx=12∫11−u2⋅14du=3∫11−u2du=3artanh⁡u+C=3artanh⁡4x+C

Note that this result is subject to the condition |4x|<1.

Question 16
?

Evaluate the integral ∫369x2−3dx.

a
9ln⁡(3+114)
b
9ln⁡(3+112)
c
3ln⁡(3+112)
d
9ln⁡(23+113+2)
e
3ln⁡(3+1123+2)
Submit

decision.explanation: An antiderivative is 9 ln(x+√(x²−3)). Evaluating from 3 to 6 gives 9 ln((6+√33)/(3+√6))=9 ln((2√3+√11)/(√3+√2)), which is option d.

after.name: Question 16
after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
{\int }_{3}^{6}\frac{9}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-3}}\,\text{d}x=3\sqrt{3}{\int }_{3}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $3$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\sqrt{3}$ | $2\sqrt{3}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{6}\frac{9}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-3}}\,\text{d}x & =3\sqrt{3}{\int }_{3}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\sqrt{3}{\int }_{\sqrt{3}}^{2\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =9{\int }_{\sqrt{3}}^{2\sqrt{3}}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =9\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u{|}_{\sqrt{3}}^{2\sqrt{3}} \\  & =9(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡2\sqrt{3}-\operatorname{arcosh}⁡\sqrt{3}) \\  & =9(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{{(2\sqrt{3})}^{2}-1})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{{(\sqrt{3})}^{2}-1})) \\  & =9(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{11})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2})) \\  & =9\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2}})\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Note that we can rewrite this integral as ∫369x2−3dx=33∫361(x3)2−1dx.

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse hyperbolic cosine, ∫1u2−1du=arcosh⁡u+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have (x3)2.

So, let's substitute u=x3. Differentiating, we get dudx=13⟹dx=3du.

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from x to u.

x 3 6
u 3 23

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫369x2−3dx=33∫361(x3)2−1dx=33∫3231u2−1⋅(3du)=9∫323duu2−1=9arcosh⁡u|323=9(arcosh⁡23−arcosh⁡3)=9(ln⁡(23+(23)2−1)−ln⁡(3+(3)2−1))=9(ln⁡(23+11)−ln⁡(3+2))=9ln⁡(23+113+2)

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Functions
content.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
{\int }_{3}^{6}\frac{9}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-3}}\,\text{d}x=3\sqrt{3}{\int }_{3}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $3$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\sqrt{3}$ | $2\sqrt{3}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{6}\frac{9}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-3}}\,\text{d}x & =3\sqrt{3}{\int }_{3}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\sqrt{3}{\int }_{\sqrt{3}}^{2\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =9{\int }_{\sqrt{3}}^{2\sqrt{3}}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =9\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u{|}_{\sqrt{3}}^{2\sqrt{3}} \\  & =9(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡2\sqrt{3}-\operatorname{arcosh}⁡\sqrt{3}) \\  & =9(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{{(2\sqrt{3})}^{2}-1})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{{(\sqrt{3})}^{2}-1})) \\  & =9(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{11})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2})) \\  & =9\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2}})\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+36}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{6})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{6})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{6}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{6}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=6\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+36}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{6})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\cdot (6\,\text{d}u) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡1-\operatorname{arsinh}⁡0 \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+\sqrt{{1}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+\sqrt{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Question 19
?

Evaluate the integral ∫061x2+36dx.

a
ln⁡(2+6)
b
ln⁡(1+2)
c
ln⁡(1+6)
d
ln⁡(2+3)
e
ln⁡(6+3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that we can rewrite this integral as ∫061x2+36dx=16∫061(x6)2+1dx.

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse hyperbolic sine,

∫1u2+1du=arsinh⁡u+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have (x6)2.

So, let's substitute u=x6. Differentiating, we get dudx=16⟹dx=6du.

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from x to u.

x 0 6
u 0 1

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫061x2+36dx=16∫061(x6)2+1dx=16∫011u2+1⋅(6du)=∫01duu2+1=arsinh⁡u|01=arsinh⁡1−arsinh⁡0=arsinh⁡1=ln⁡(1+12+1)=ln⁡(1+2)

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Functions
content.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+36}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{6})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{6})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{6}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{6}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=6\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+36}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{6})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\cdot (6\,\text{d}u) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡1-\operatorname{arsinh}⁡0 \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+\sqrt{{1}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+\sqrt{2})\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=x/2. The integral becomes 8∫₀²du/√(u²+1)=8[arsinh(u)]₀²=8 ln(2+√5), which is option a.

after.name: Question 20
after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{8}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4}}\,\text{d}x=4{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $2$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{8}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4}}\,\text{d}x & =4{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\cdot (2\,\text{d}u) \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}} \\  & =8\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =8\operatorname{arsinh}⁡2-8\operatorname{arsinh}⁡0 \\  & =8\operatorname{arsinh}⁡2 \\  & =8\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+\sqrt{{2}^{2}+1}) \\  & =8\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+\sqrt{5})\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Functions
content.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{8}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4}}\,\text{d}x=4{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $2$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{8}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4}}\,\text{d}x & =4{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\cdot (2\,\text{d}u) \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}} \\  & =8\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =8\operatorname{arsinh}⁡2-8\operatorname{arsinh}⁡0 \\  & =8\operatorname{arsinh}⁡2 \\  & =8\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+\sqrt{{2}^{2}+1}) \\  & =8\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+\sqrt{5})\end{aligned}
$$
